```{r setup}
library(tbprogress)
```

## Who this is for, and the question it answers

`tbprogress` is for a **public-health analyst or policy student** who needs to
judge how a country's tuberculosis (TB) burden is trending. It is built around
one question:

> **Is a country's TB burden falling fast enough to meet the WHO End TB
> milestones, and how does it compare with its region?**

The WHO End TB Strategy asks every country to cut the TB incidence rate and the
number of TB deaths by set percentages compared with **2015**. The package
bundles WHO's estimates for 215 countries (2000-2023), turns the milestones into
a yearly "path", and provides a Shiny app to explore where each country stands.

## 1. Install the package

Install from GitHub with the `remotes` package. You need R 4.1 or newer.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-avat0006-ai")
```

## 2. Launch the app

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(tbprogress)
run_tb_app()
```

The app opens in your web browser. It reads only the data inside the installed
package, so there is nothing else to download. To stop it, press the stop button
in RStudio or press `Esc` / `Ctrl + C` in the R console.

## 3. Use the app

The sidebar has five controls. They all feed the same question:

| Control | What it does | When to change it |
|:--------|:-------------|:------------------|
| **1. Indicator** | Chooses the burden to track: *incidence rate* (new cases per 100,000 people) or *TB deaths* (number per year). | To check the incidence milestone and the deaths milestone separately; a country can be on track for one but not the other. |
| **2. Countries** | Up to five countries, searchable and grouped by WHO region. | To compare countries you care about. |
| **3. Assess progress in year** | The year the status table and peer chart judge against 2015. | To ask "was this country ever on track?" by moving back in time. |
| **4. Compare with the WHO region median** | Adds the typical country in the same WHO region as a dotted line. | To see whether a country is doing better or worse than its neighbours. |
| **5. Hide countries under 1 million people** (Peers tab only) | Removes tiny populations whose percentages swing wildly. | Leave on for a readable chart; switch off to see everyone. |

A suggested route through the app:

1. Start on the **Progress** tab with the default countries and the incidence
   indicator. Read the headline strip first: how many are on track?
2. Look at the trajectory chart to see *why*. Is a country's line below the
   dashed orange path (ahead) or above it (behind)?
3. Check the status table for exact numbers.
4. Switch to **Peers** to see whether the country is unusual for its region.
5. Change the indicator to **TB deaths** and repeat. The answer is often
   different.

The **Guide** tab inside the app repeats this information, so you never have to
leave it.

## 4. Interpret the outputs

The rest of this vignette reproduces the app's outputs with the package
functions, so you can see exactly what they show. We use four countries with
contrasting stories.

```{r choose}
countries <- c("Kenya", "South Africa", "India", "Brazil")
```

### The status table

`tb_progress_summary()` compares each country's reduction since 2015 with the
reduction the WHO milestone path requires by the assessment year.

```{r summary}
inc <- tb_progress_summary(indicator = "incidence", assess_year = 2023,
                           countries = countries)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Country = inc$country,
    `2015 rate` = inc$baseline_value,
    `2023 rate` = inc$current_value,
    `Reduction (%)` = round(inc$reduction_pct, 1),
    `Needed (%)` = round(inc$required_reduction_pct, 1),
    `Gap (pct. points)` = round(inc$gap_pp, 1),
    Status = as.character(inc$status),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

How to read each column:

- **Reduction** is how much the incidence rate has fallen since 2015. A negative
  value means it has *risen*.
- **Needed** is the reduction the WHO milestone path requires by 2023. WHO sets
  milestones only for 2020, 2025, 2030 and 2035, so the path between them is a
  straight line (`tb_required_reduction(2023, "incidence")` is
  `r tb_required_reduction(2023, "incidence")`%).
- **Gap** is reduction minus needed. Positive means ahead of the path.
- **Status** is **On track** when the reduction is at least what is needed,
  **Behind** when the burden is falling but too slowly, **Rising** when it is
  higher than in 2015, and **No data** when WHO has no usable 2015 baseline.

```{r headline, include = FALSE}
n_on <- sum(inc$status == "On track")
best <- inc[which.max(inc$reduction_pct), ]
```

In this example, **`r n_on` of the `r nrow(inc)` countries** are on track for the
incidence milestone, and the largest reduction is in **`r best$country`**
(`r round(best$reduction_pct, 1)`%).

### The trajectory chart

```{r trajectory}
plot_tb_trajectory(indicator = "incidence", countries = countries)
```

Each panel rescales one country so that **2015 = 100**, which lets countries
with very different rates sit on one footing.

- The **solid blue line** is the country. Where it ends *below* the dashed
  orange line, the country is ahead of the milestones.
- The **dashed orange line** is the WHO milestone path (dots mark 2020, 2025 and
  2030). It continues to 2030 so you can see how far there is still to go.
- The **dotted grey line** is the median country in the same WHO region.

This links straight back to the question: a country can only meet the End TB
milestones if its blue line follows the orange path down. A line that is flat
or rising is on course to miss them.

### The peer chart

```{r peers}
plot_tb_peers(indicator = "incidence", assess_year = 2023, highlight = countries)
```

Each dot is a country, grouped by WHO region, and its horizontal position is the
reduction since 2015. The dashed orange line is the reduction needed by 2023, so
**dots to its right are on track**. Your highlighted countries are labelled in
blue. Use this chart to judge whether a country is typical of its region or an
outlier: a country that is on track in a region where almost nobody is stands out.

### Repeat for deaths

The deaths milestone is stricter than the incidence milestone for the same year,
and the picture often changes:

```{r deaths}
dea <- tb_progress_summary(indicator = "mortality", assess_year = 2023,
                           countries = countries)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Country = dea$country,
    `Reduction (%)` = round(dea$reduction_pct, 1),
    `Needed (%)` = round(dea$required_reduction_pct, 1),
    Status = as.character(dea$status),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

## 5. Caveats

- The numbers are **modelled WHO estimates**. The uncertainty intervals are not
  in this dataset, so treat a gap of a few percentage points as "about on the
  path" rather than a firm verdict.
- A percentage change from a **zero baseline** is undefined, so such countries
  (and countries with no WHO estimate, such as North Korea for deaths) show as
  **No data**.
- Very **small populations** produce volatile percentages, which is why the peer
  chart hides countries under one million people by default.
- The **region median** gives every country equal weight, regardless of
  population.

## 6. Using the functions without the app

Everything in the app is available programmatically:

```{r functions}
# All countries, deaths, 2023
all_dea <- tb_progress_summary(indicator = "mortality", assess_year = 2023)
table(all_dea$status)

# The yearly index behind the trajectory chart
head(tb_index(indicator = "incidence", countries = "Kenya"), 3)
```

See the [function reference](../reference/index.html) for details, and
`?tb_burden` for a description of every variable and the data's source and
terms of use.
